The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. But “whatever” is a strange word. It implies freedom, yet also a blankness. If I let my mind wander, where does it go? To the morning light, the smell of coffee, the unfinished list of tasks, the distant sound of traffic. The mind is not a river; it is more like a weather system, made of currents and pressures, suddenly sunny and then overcast. Trying to catch it on the page is like trying to photograph a cloud. I think of all the words I have used in my life, all the sentences I have built and abandoned, and how each one has left a tiny sediment of meaning. Now I am asked to produce a thousand of them, not for any purpose, just to see what emerges. This is a kind of freewriting, a practice I have always found both liberating and terrifying. Liberating because no one is judging; terrifying because no one is judging. Without a criterion, the writing becomes a mirror, and mirrors are honest.

Freedom is a paradox. When I have no constraints, I invent them. I worry about word count, about rhythm, about saying something true. The page is white and infinite; it is like standing in a desert. In a desert, you notice every stone, every shadow. On a blank page, you notice every hesitation. I remember a writing teacher who said, “If you are stuck, write about being stuck.” That advice has saved me hundreds of times. It works because it turns blockage into material. It also works because it reminds me that the process of writing is not separate from the content of writing. The mind is not a vessel that empties into sentences; it is formed by the sentences themselves. Each word I choose changes the next choice, and the next, and the next. So “whatever comes to you” is not a command to receive a pre-existing thought; it is an invitation to think on paper, to discover the thought in the act of making it. That is why writing is so difficult: it is not transcription, but composition. The thought does not exist before the sentence. It exists in the sentence, and it can be altered by a single comma.

There is a particular quality to words when they are written without intention. They become intimate. They show the seams of your thinking, the little loops and repetitions. I notice that my own mind often jumps from the ordinary to the abstract. A car door slams outside, and I think about how every moment is lost the moment it is lived. Then I think about how a sentence can hold a moment, like a jar catching rain. But the jar is full of holes; language is always approximate. We say “I love you” and mean something far more complicated. We say “I am fine” and mean the opposite. The literary critic George Steiner wrote that language can only deal meaningfully with a special, restricted segment of reality. The rest is silence, or music, or nonsense. This is not a failure; it is the very reason we keep writing. We are always trying to say what cannot be said, and the attempt itself makes us human. Even a shopping list is an attempt to impose order on chaos. Even a text message is a small ark sent across the flood of ordinary time.

I think about the technology of writing itself. A thousand words is not very long. The word count of a novel is eighty thousand. A thousand words is a blog post, a short essay, a long letter. It is also the length of a chapter in some books, or the length of a single scene in a movie. How many lives have been changed by a thousand words? Maybe a speech that ended a war, or began one. Maybe a letter from a lover, read and reread until the paper is soft. Maybe a list of names, each one a world, read aloud at a memorial. The same number of words can be a curse or a blessing, a diagnosis or a prayer. I think about the pace at which we consume words now—scrolling, tapping, skimming—and I wonder what it does to us. We are awash in language, and yet we are lonely. Perhaps because we mistake information for communication. A thousand words can be dumped in a minute, but it takes a lifetime to mean. So when I am asked to write whatever comes to me, I want to slow down. I want to make each sentence breathe. The reader is not a machine; time flows through them as through me. We are both here, in this moment of words, and the words are the only bridge.

I also think about the word count itself. Why a thousand? Why not seven hundred, or two thousand, or a hundred and eleven? There is something round and ancient about a thousand. It is the number of nights in the *Arabian Nights*, the number of soldiers in a Spartan phalanx, the number of cranes folded for a wish. It is a number small enough to hold in the mind and large enough to demand a commitment. A thousand words forces a shape: a beginning, a middle, an end. It asks for patience and then rewards it. The writer must wander enough to find something, but not wander so far that the reader is lost. It is almost exactly the length of this piece, and I feel that length now as a physical pressure, like carrying a tray full of glasses. If I am too slow, the words may spill; if I am too fast, they will be empty. I hold them carefully. I try to keep them balanced.

What has come to me? This. I did not plan it. I started with a blank page, with a simple instruction, and I let the current carry me. There is a strange pleasure in this kind of writing. It is like swimming in water that is deeper than you thought. You cannot touch the bottom, so you have to trust your body to float. At first you flail, then you find a rhythm. The rhythm is not yours; it is the water’s. But in the water, you are also the water’s. I think this is what the poet means by “inspiration”—not a bolt from the sky, but a slow breathing in. Inspiration is respiration, an exchange with the world. Every word I write is borrowed from a language that existed before me and will continue after me. I am a temporary custodian of these sounds and signs. I might misuse them, but they forgive me. They are patient. They have been used to curse and to bless, to lie and to love, to sign treaties and to make grocery lists. They will survive my mistakes, as they have survived everyone’s. So I write without fear, because fear is just a word, and words are just vessels, and the sea is infinite.
